name: Hamilton
summary: Freedmen established homes in Hamilton after the Civil War. The community centred on Mount Zion Methodist Episcopal Church and nearby schools for African American children.

name: Grand United Order of Odd Fellows
Galilean Fisherman Fraternal Hall
summary: Formed by Hamilton residents as a mutual aid society, since Black residents were often denied access to insurance and credit. Its building on West Virginia Avenue no longer stands.

name: Brownsville (Harmony) School
summary: Opened in 1887 to serve Black students from the Jefferson and Mt. Gilead school districts. Converted into a private residence in 1925.

name: Brownsville (Swampoodle)
summary: A post-Civil War African American village, also called Swampoodle because of its flood-prone land. It grew around a schoolhouse and church. The school opened in 1887 and closed to students in 1925, when it became a residence.

name: The Color Line
summary: African Americans did not begin to settle in Purcellville until after the Civil War. Beginning in the late nineteenth century, the African Americans that moved to Purcellville settled in neighborhoods within the south-central section of town, away from the White neighborhoods. G Street became known as 'the color line', since this street separated the Black and White neighborhoods.
